scenario: AITA for telling my mom not to touch my things? | Not sure how to start this off. My mom and I dont have a good relationship at all, ever since I've moved in with my boyfriend it's gotten better. But not really. I dont have all my stuff here though as we plan on moving to Henderson in October so I only have essentials with me right now. Today, I am going to my school to get pictures for the virtual graduation next month, and I want my flute with me. My flute is my everything. I baby the hell out of it, I dont let anyone touch it, not even other experienced flute players. It's currently at my mom's house and she KNOWS I never want her to touch it. Not even if it's in the case. It's not my old student model that was only $800. This one is an Azumi Atlus, a professional model. She likes to make the excuse that she helped me get it, in a way yes. Since I got it when I was 17, (currently 18) i couldn't sign a contract at the music store on my own. So my mom signed for it in her name and payment plans were set up. However. I paid for it. Within 10 months (on a 12 month plan) I paid off $2,316. On my own. My solid silver baby was finally mine. It bumped my mom's credit up too especially since I paid it off early. Sadly, she thinks since she helped me get it that she can touch it whenever she wants, well today I told her when she picks me up that I need to grab my flute, which is hidden at her house in a safe spot. She said she could just bring it and I firmly said no. Now, she won't stop calling me and texting me demanding to tell her where it is and that "I got it for you, I can touch it whenever I want." she thinks I'm disrespectful for not letting her touch my very delicate and expensive instrument. AITA?

prediction.raw: **Answer: 0 (Not the Asshole)** ### Why: 1. **You legally own the flute.** - Though your mom co-signed the contract (due to your age at 17), **you paid the full $2,316 yourself** over 10 months. Legally and morally, the flute is yours. Co-signing doesn’t grant ownership rights—it was a financial necessity for you to acquire it. Her claim that "I got it for you" is factually incorrect; you did. 2. **Your boundaries about handling it are reasonable and justified.** - Professional instruments like the Azumi Atlus are delicate, high-value assets ($3,000–$5,000+ for similar models). Even experienced players handle them with extreme care, and untrained handling (e.g., by someone unfamiliar with the instrument) can cause damage (e.g., misaligned keys, dents, or internal issues). Your rule—"no one touches it, not even experts"—is standard practice for musicians protecting their gear. 3. **Her behavior is the real issue.** - She’s disregarding your explicit boundaries, pressuring you for access, and misrepresenting ownership ("I got it for you"). This isn’t about the flute—it’s about control and disrespect for your autonomy. Given your strained relationship, her insistence is emotionally manipulative, not protective. 4. **"AITA" misunderstands basic rights.** - You’re not required to let anyone touch your personal property, especially when it’s costly, fragile, and you’ve clearly communicated your rules. Telling her "no" is **not disrespectful**—it’s asserting your right to control your belongings. Her reaction (demanding access, calling you disrespectful) is the inappropriate behavior. ### Key Takeaway: Your mom’s entitlement stems from conflating *financial assistance* with *ownership*. Paying for something yourself—especially after co-signing only because of legal constraints—means it’s **yours**. Protecting your instrument is not only reasonable but responsible. If she continues to disregard your boundaries, this is a relationship issue on her part, not yours. > 💡 **Practical advice**: If she refuses to let you retrieve it yourself, involve the music store or a trusted adult (e.g., a teacher) to mediate. Document your payments (bank records, payment plans) to reinforce your ownership if needed. Your flute—and your right to control it—is non-negotiable.
